items.title: What a hospital transfer reveals about Pakistan’s two top courts
items.description: In short · a 1-minute primer The rules changed In 2024 and 2025 parliament changed the Constitution. The government got more control over who becomes a judge, and a new top court was created next to the Supreme Court. A test case In August 2026 the Supreme Court ordered that jailed former PM Imran Khan be taken to a private hospital. He was taken to a government hospital instead. The new court then called for the records of his cases. The argument The writer argues that the changes leave it unclear which top court has the final word, and that this uncertainty affects everyone who goes to court. Colour key for the numbered explainers: Constitution & law Courts & bodies People Places Legal idea When the 26th and 27th Amendments 1 were forced through the assemblies, overhauling the country’s judicial system without debate or discourse, many of us saw the writing on the wall: Pakistan’s judiciary may have been far from perfect, but it seemed to be heading into bleaker terrain. 1 Constitution & law The 26th and 27th Amendments Changes to Pakistan’s Constitution passed by parliament. The 26th (October 2024) changed how judges are chosen: a parliamentary committee now selects the Chief Justice from the three most senior judges, and parliamentarians sit on the Judicial Commission. The 27th (November 2025) created the Federal Constitutional Court and allowed high court judges to be transferred without their consent. Justices Mansoor Ali Shah and Athar Minallah resigned from the Supreme Court after it was passed. Opinion Opinion · Zainab Shahid 27th Amendment: The end of an era News News What is the 26th Constitutional Amendment? The post-amendment judiciary was fashioned to fulfill short-term political objectives with no consideration for the possibility of doing long-term systemic harm. Two problems have been created as a result. The first outcome is the dismantling of judicial independence. This is a consequence of executive-controlled judicial appointments and promotions under the reconfigured Judicial Commission of Pakistan 2 and the Article 200 power to transfer judges 3 without their consent or remove them from office if consent is not given to the transfer. A prominent example of the exercise of these powers is the scattering of three of the six Islamabad High Court judges 4 who had filed petitions against illegal surveillance of their homes and executive interference in judicial affairs. While elected officials provide input on judicial appointments in other countries as well, the matrix of direct executive control over judicial appointments along with insecurity of judicial tenure is unique to Pakistan’s new system. 2 Courts & bodies Judicial Commission of Pakistan The panel that picks judges for the high courts and the Supreme Court. Since 2024 it has 13 members, 5 of them judges. The others include the federal law minister, the Attorney General, four members of parliament and a senior lawyer. News News What is the 26th Constitutional Amendment? 3 Constitution & law Article 200: moving judges The constitutional rule on moving a high court judge to another province’s high court. Judges used to have to agree. Since the 27th Amendment, a judge can be transferred on the Judicial Commission’s recommendation without consent, and a judge who declines can be treated as retired. Opinion Opinion · Anwar Mansoor Khan Judicial disaster News News Law ministry notifies transfer of 3 IHC judges to other high courts 4 People The six IHC judges In March 2024, six Islamabad High Court judges wrote to the Supreme Judicial Council alleging interference in judicial affairs by intelligence agencies, including surveillance. In April 2026, three of them, Justices Mohsin Akhtar Kayani, Babar Sattar and Saman Rafat Imtiaz, were transferred to the Lahore, Peshawar and Sindh high courts on the Judicial Commission’s recommendation. News News IHC judges detail ‘brazen meddling’ in letter to Supreme Judicial Council The second outcome is the creation of a supposed dual apex system and the replacement of the Supreme Court through the creation of a Federal Constitutional Court 5 (comprising a bench appointed directly by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister under Article 175A(3) of the Constitution) as the apex court for constitutional matters. 5 Courts & bodies Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) A new court created in November 2025. It has the final word on what the Constitution means, and its rulings bind every other court, including the Supreme Court. Its first Chief Justice and judges were appointed by the President on the Prime Minister’s advice. Later appointments go through the Judicial Commission. Opinion Opinion · Asad-ul-Mulk Grundnorm News News Who is the first chief justice of the Federal Constitutional Court? How the top courts changed Before November 2025 Supreme Court Final word on everything, including the Constitution ↓ hears appeals from High Courts ↓ Lower courts After the 27th Amendment Federal Constitutional Court Final word on the Constitution. Its rulings bind every court. Supreme Court Ordinary civil and criminal appeals ⟵ The FCC can call for the record of a case in any court if it considers that it raises a substantial constitutional question (Art. 175E(5)) ↓ both hear appeals from High Courts Judges can now be transferred without consent ↓ Lower courts Simplified. Under Article 189 as amended, the FCC’s decisions bind all other courts, including the Supreme Court. Both problems are clearly exemplified by the continuing judicial chaos around the Supreme Court order to shift Imran Khan to Shifa International Hospital. The Imran Khan episode, step by step ✓ 18 August 2026 The Supreme Court orders that Imran Khan be moved from Adiala Jail to Shifa International, a private hospital. ✕ Two nights later He is taken to PIMS, a government hospital, and returned to jail the same night. The government says this was a security decision. … Contempt petitions filed His family files petitions in the Supreme Court alleging the order was not complied with. They are fixed for hearing on 16 September. ⇄ 15 September In separate appeals by Adiala Jail prisoners, the FCC invokes Article 175E(5) and calls for the records of cases concerning Khan’s medical treatment. ‖ Next hearing The Supreme Court observes that matters under ordinary criminal laws remain within its jurisdiction, and adjourns for three weeks at the Attorney General’s request. ? Now Which court has jurisdiction over these cases is still to be decided. Supreme Court FCC Government Over months of deliberate delays, various appeals, petitions for suspension of sentences, contempt of court applications, and other proceedings remained pending at the Islamabad High Court and the Supreme Court. Then on 18 August 2026, the Supreme Court directed that former Prime Minister Imran Khan be shifted from Adiala Jail 6 to Shifa International Hospital. Instead, two nights later, as the world’s press waited outside Shifa, he was taken to PIMS Hospital 7 and returned to Adiala Jail within hours. In other words, when faced with a rare, undesirable order, the state exhibited noncompliance. And when Khan’s family filed contempt petitions 8 against the state’s noncompliance with the order, the Supreme Court chose not to fix them for hearing until 16 September, thereby kicking the confrontation down the road instead of defending its order. 6 Places Adiala Jail The main jail in Rawalpindi, where Imran Khan has been held since 2023. News News SC orders moving jailed ex-PM Imran Khan to Shifa International Hospital 7 Places PIMS and Shifa PIMS is a government hospital in Islamabad. Shifa International, named in the Supreme Court’s order, is a private hospital in the same city. The government said taking Khan to PIMS was a security decision. News News Govt says shifting Imran to Pims instead of Shifa a ‘security decision’ 8 Legal idea Contempt petition A request asking a court to punish someone for disobeying its order. Here, Khan’s family filed petitions alleging that the Supreme Court’s order had not been complied with. The petitions are pending. Then, on 15 September, the Attorney General 9 , while appearing before the FCC in separate (unusually fast-tracked) appeals filed by Adiala Jail prisoners, argued that the Supreme Court no longer has the authority to protect fundamental rights, even the rights of prisoners. In response, the FCC invoked its powers under Article 175E(5) 10 to unilaterally summon the record of all cases concerning Imran Khan’s access to medical treatment and connected matters, thereby arrogating jurisdiction over the case to itself. 9 People Attorney General The government’s top lawyer, who argues the state’s side in court. 10 Constitution & law Article 175E(5): the call-up power A new clause allowing the FCC, if it considers that a case involves a substantial question about interpreting the Constitution, to call for the record of a case pending before any court and make such order as it thinks fit. It does not need a referral from another court. Editorial Editorial Court vs court News News FCC summons Supreme Court’s case records on Imran’s hospital transfer Having been summarily deprived of jurisdiction, the Supreme Court held its own hearing wherein it pointed out that disputes arising out of ordinary criminal statutes, such as the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898 and the Contempt of Court Ordinance 2003, and subordinate legislation, such as the Pakistan Prison Rules 1978, remain within the appellate jurisdiction 11 of the Supreme Court even after the 27th Amendment. 11 Legal idea Appellate jurisdiction The power to hear appeals, meaning to review a lower court’s decision and confirm or overturn it. In this matter the Supreme Court observed that disputes under ordinary criminal laws and the Prison Rules remain within its appellate jurisdiction. The question is pending before the courts. News News SC dismayed by FCC demand for Imran’s case record The Supreme Court questioned the effect of the FCC’s order to transfer the cases as the “constitutional scheme does not position either of the two apex courts as an appellate forum to each other; rather, it treats both as coordinate courts exercising clearly demarcated jurisdictions over distinct classes of matters.” It then adjourned the matter for three weeks at the Attorney General’s request. As such, the question of which court has appellate jurisdiction for matters related to prisoners remains unresolved not just for Imran Khan, but for every prisoner in the country. The question of which court has appellate jurisdiction for matters related to prisoners remains unresolved not just for Imran Khan, but for every prisoner in the country. While this episode may appear farcical, it is an inevitable outcome of the way Pakistan’s judiciary was redesigned last year. In systems with separate constitutional courts 12 , those courts either have formally or customarily circumscribed appellate jurisdiction or are generally restricted to the judicial review of parliamentary or delegated legislation. These constitutional courts are not designed to hear any and all cases in which a provision of the constitution is involved nor are they meant to deprive all other superior courts of their jurisdiction over all matters involving fundamental rights. 12 Legal idea Constitutional courts elsewhere Countries such as Germany, Italy and South Africa have a separate constitutional court. These courts mostly check whether laws are constitutional. Everyday criminal and civil appeals stay with the regular courts. Opinion Opinion · Reema Omer Kelsen’s return The reason for this is simple: as any legal practitioner can tell you, any dispute, whether it is a criminal, civil, administrative or property matter can involve fundamental rights or safeguards that are guaranteed by the Constitution. Even tax disputes involve the interpretation of constitutional provisions, albeit within the ambit of established precedent set by superior courts. All courts are supposed to uphold and enforce the fundamental rights and guarantees contained in the Constitution. The need for this is clearly evidenced across a range of disputes: property disputes involve the fundamental right to property, criminal appeals involve the right to due process and fair trial, Pakistan Electronic Crimes Act 13 disputes involve the right to free speech, employment disputes concern the right to equal treatment and so on. 13 Constitution & law PECA: Pakistan’s cybercrime law The Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), passed in 2016. Changes in January 2025 made spreading “false or fake information” online a crime. Journalists’ unions and rights groups, including Amnesty International, criticised the changes. News News NA passes controversial Peca amendment bill The FCC was hurriedly transplanted into our common law legal system 14 even though the forced distinction between constitutional and fundamental rights adjudication versus ordinary criminal and civil adjudication that underpinned the creation of a separate constitutional court does not exist in common law traditions. 14 Legal idea Common law The legal system Pakistan inherited from Britain, also used in India. Judges build the law case by case, and the same courts handle both ordinary and constitutional questions. Opinion Opinion · Usama Khawar Pakistan has a supreme court. Then it built a supremacist one. The 27th Amendment’s provisions reveal the true nature of the powers endowed to the FCC and the role intended for it by the amenders. The original jurisdiction and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, under the previous Articles 184 and 186 15 , were transferred wholesale to the FCC. Appeals originating from Article 199 writ jurisdiction 16 were also transferred. Article 175E(5) relied upon by the FCC in the Imran Khan cases, empowers the FCC to, “if it considers that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, call for the record of any case pending before any court and make such order in the case as it thinks fit.” ‘Any court’ naturally includes the Supreme Court. 15 Constitution & law Articles 184 and 186 Two powers the Supreme Court used to have. Article 184 let it take up cases directly, including the public-interest cases it was known for. Article 186 let the President ask for its legal opinion. Both now belong to the FCC. News News What new changes has the National Assembly made to the 27th Amendment bill? 16 Constitution & law Article 199: writs The power of high courts to order government bodies to act lawfully, for example to free someone held illegally. Appeals against these orders now go to the FCC instead of the Supreme Court. Article 175F(1)(a) seemingly empowers the legislature to expand the appellate jurisdiction of the FCC at the expense of the Supreme Court’s through ordinary legislation. Article 189 17 states that the decisions of the FCC shall bind all other courts in the country, explicitly including the Supreme Court. The text of the amendment does not suggest that a co-equal apex court was being created. 17 Constitution & law Article 189: whose rulings count The rule that lower courts must follow higher courts’ rulings. It now says every court, including the Supreme Court, must follow the FCC. News News Federal Constitutional Court asserts it is not bound by Supreme Court rulings The Supreme Court might argue, as its Chief Justice did, that the, “constitutional scheme does not position either of the two apex courts as an appellate forum to each other; rather, it treats both as coordinate courts exercising clearly demarcated jurisdictions over distinct classes of matters.” It could even argue that despite the 27th Amendment, the Article 185 appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in criminal matters is entirely separate from the constitutional interpretation mandate of the FCC. It could also argue that the implementation of specific standards in the archaic Prison Rules obviously does not present a constitutional question requiring intervention from the FCC. But all of this misses the point. If no other court including the Supreme Court can adjudicate cases involving questions of constitutional rights—and constitutional rights remain intertwined with most disputes—the FCC can logically reframe any matter as a constitutional matter and assume exclusive jurisdiction over it. This includes ordinary appellate matters and not just those originating as writ petitions under Article 199 which have already been transferred to the FCC. Since there is no clear method to resolve boundary or jurisdictional disputes and the power to transfer a case to the FCC does not require a referral by the Supreme Court (with instead a unilateral call-up power being exercised by the FCC), the power to remove the Supreme Court from the play lies wholly with the FCC. Any time the Supreme Court issues an adverse decision, the FCC may assume jurisdiction and rehear the matter. The power to remove the Supreme Court from the play lies wholly with the FCC. That is exactly what happened in the Imran Khan criminal appeals and contempt cases. The two arguments relied on by advocates of the 27th Amendment were the need to decrease case backlog and curb judicial overreach. While the case backlog was reported as climbing in the SC’s own assessment, the amendments have created an unpredictable and arbitrary system with competing courts with no certainty as to procedure, jurisdiction, or finality of decisions. The only success story is that via the FCC, the executive has successfully curtailed ‘judicial overreach’ by controlling outcomes through a hand-picked court. The 27th Amendment judiciary was architected to create a winner-takes-all system. Now, if you manage to take control of the executive, whether by democratic or undemocratic means, there is nothing to prevent you from packing courts, sidelining independent judges and denying access to justice to both political opponents and critics of government policy. The 27th Amendment judiciary was architected to create a winner-takes-all system. This matters. Where the writer says it shows up Long sentences for human rights defenders over posts online Bail orders and detainees’ cases Listing and hearing of political prisoners’ cases Protection for journalists Gender justice rulings Tax, land acquisition and environment cases Eroded judicial independence, denuded writ of the courts, and jurisdictional uncertainty does not only lead to unjust outcomes in cases involving former prime ministers, it shows up as judicial paralysis when human rights defenders and lawyers, such as Imaan and Hadi 18 , are given seventeen-year sentences over tweets that offend the state. It shows up as bail orders being ignored and secret FIRs being used to play cat-and-mouse games with state detainees. It shows up as the deliberate non-listing and non-hearing of cases involving political prisoners. It shows up as a lack of protection for journalists hounded by state authorities. It shows up as the regressive reinterpretation of settled law in gender justice matters 19 . It shows up as favorable decisions for the state in taxation, land acquisition, and environmental matters when special interests are at stake. In a system like this, the powerful always win and ordinary citizens always lose. 18 People Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha Lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari and her husband, lawyer Hadi Ali Chattha, were convicted under PECA by an Islamabad court in January 2026 in a case over social media posts and sentenced to 17 years each. On 17 September 2026 the Supreme Court suspended the sentences pending their appeals. Police arrested them the same day in a separate case. Both matters are before the courts. News News SC suspends Imaan, Hadi’s sentences in social media posts case News News Journalists, lawyers condemn Imaan, Hadi’s rearrest hours after bail 19 Legal idea Gender justice at the FCC Former Supreme Court judge Syed Mansoor Ali Shah has written in Dawn criticising a recent FCC judgment on workplace harassment. He argues that it narrowed the meaning of harassment and departed from earlier precedent. Opinion Opinion · Justice (retd) Syed Mansoor Ali Shah The court that could not see In a system like this, the powerful always win and ordinary citizens always lose. items.title: DG ISPR says Pakistani troops present in Saudi Arabia 'for decades' across multiple domains
items.description: Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said that Pakistani troops are in Saudi Arabia, adding that they had been in the kingdom “for decades” and across multiple domains. The military spokesperson made these remarks during an interview with CNN correspondent Ivan Watson, who posted a small clip on his X account. “I can confirm that the forces of Pakistan are already there (Saudi Arabia),” Lt Gen Chaudhry said. Watson then sought a confirmation that Pakistani troops were already on the ground in Saudi Arabia as part of the Makkah Defence Alliance between Pakistan, the kingdom and Turkiye. To that, the military spokesperson replied, “Pakistan troops have been there for decades […] The Makkah alliance is not something that has come out in a vacuum. So there is a sustained diplomatic, political, military and people-to-people relationship between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia. So, I can share with you that Pakistani forces, in multiple capabilities and domains, are already there.” Lt Gen Chaudhry’s remarks come after Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye agreed to the deployment of military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Riyadh on Monday. The three countries had held an emergency meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) of the Makkah Defence Alliance to address the security developments and threats facing Saudi Arabia. “The committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the parties, thereby enhancing readiness, military integration, and the collective capacity to confront and counter threats,” a statement issued by the Foreign Office after the meeting said. While the statement did not specifically name any threat, the development comes against the backdrop of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in the Yemen conflict. Separately, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, joined Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ via telephone the same day and said Saudi Arabia had made “gains and recovered some areas” in Yemen in the ongoing fighting with the Houthis. When asked about a possible operational role by Pakistan and Turkiye, the defence minister replied that both nations had a “presence in theatre”, but only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. “Whatever assistance they require is being provided. But right now, the Turkish and Pakistani armies are playing a supportive role,” he said, noting that Pakistan was involved in reconnaissance. Asif had earlier also reaffirmed that Pakistan would “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalated. The defence minister had said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. The Makkah defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. On Sept 25, the military chiefs of alliance members Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia met in Riyadh for urgently convened talks under the pact in light of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sept 18, Lt Gen Chaudhry had expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, saying Pakistan will go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”.

items.title: Qui contrôle le détroit de Bab el-Mandeb ?
items.description: En début de semaine, les forces gouvernementales yéménites, assistées par l'Arabie saoudite, ont lancé une contre-offensive visant à récupérer les territoires capturés par les Houthis en septembre dans le Sud du pays. Lundi 5 octobre, Aden a affirmé avoir repris le contrôle de la ville portuaire de Mocha et de Dhubab, plus au Sud, ce que les Houthis démentent. Les Houthis contestent toute perte de contrôle de Mocha, sur la mer Rouge. Selon un chercheur du Sana'a Center, Salah Ali Salah, le groupe serait parvenu à « absorber l'élan initial » des forces gouvernementales autour de Dhubab et de la bande côtière. L'Institute for the Study of War considère que les Houthis ont, du moins pour l'instant, stoppé l'avancée des forces alignées sur le gouvernement yéménite, après avoir procédé à des retraits tactiques pour se replier sur des positions fortifiées en terrain plus favorable, aux abords de Mocha Iran Update, October 6, 2026 , Institute for the Study of War.'> 1 . 1/7 Yemen’s western coast looks very different this morning. Government-aligned forces made rapid advances around Dhubab and the coastal strip. However, field information indicates that the Houthis managed to absorb the initial momentum. pic.twitter.com/TC99ANTUA4 — Salah Ali Salah (@Salah_Ali_Salah) October 6, 2026 En plus de la côte, les affrontements entre les combattants houthistes et les forces du gouvernement yéménite se concentrent dans les hauteurs du district d'al-Waziiya, entre Mocha et Taïz, une ville située à près de 90 kilomètres à l'est de Mocha. Taïz, la troisième ville la plus peuplée du pays, occupe une position de pivot entre le nord contrôlé par les Houthis et le sud contrôlé par le gouvernement. Celle-ci pourrait se trouver encerclée par le groupe, qui cherche à couper la route la reliant à Aden. Une dégradation des positions gouvernementales dans le Sud du pays pourrait conduire à une implication plus directe de l’Arabie saoudite dans la guerre. Riyad a jusqu’à présent surtout offert du soutien aérien aux forces yéménites, et le pays a lui-même bénéficié du soutien des services de renseignement et de l'aide au ciblage de l'armée américaine How the Houthis Triumphed on the Red Sea and Sparked a New War in Yemen », The New York Times , 6 octobre 2026.'> 2 . La coalition dirigée par l’Arabie saoudite mobiliserait, selon Riyad, 100 avions de combat. Le niveau d'engagement reste toutefois, pour l'heure, très en retrait au sol par rapport à l'intervention lancée en 2015. Pour Riyad, l’un des principaux objectifs de cette opération est de reprendre le contrôle du détroit de Bab el-Mandeb, vital pour les exportations saoudiennes de pétrole, et d’affaiblir les capacités des Houthistes à mener des frappes de longue portée. Lundi 5, la Turquie et le Pakistan ont également annoncé le déploiement de forces en Arabie saoudite, dont le rôle n’a pas été précisé, dans le cadre de l’Accord de défense de La Mecque, signé en août. L’article Qui contrôle le détroit de Bab el-Mandeb ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: PCB confirms window for HBL PSL 12
items.description: The 12th edition of the HBL Pakistan Super League will be held from March 18 to May 2 next year, the Pakistan Cricket Board announced on Thursday. The window was finalised following consultations with the owners and representatives of the eight franchises at a meeting of the PSL governing council in London on Sept 1, according to the PCB. The board said details of the schedule, venues and ticketing arrangements would be announced later, while the next phase of squad-building will include direct signings, player retentions, a trade window and the player auction. PSL 12 will follow an expanded 2026 season in which the league featured eight teams for the first time following the addition of Hyderabad Kingsmen and the Rawalpindiz franchises. The 2026 edition also saw the PSL move from the draft system to a player auction for the first time. The inaugural auction, held in February, saw 103 players sold to the eight franchises. The PCB had subsequently said that players retained or acquired at the auction would be on two-year contracts covering the 11th and 12th editions, with franchises allowed to retain up to seven players for the next season. The 2026 season ended with Peshawar Zalmi claiming their second PSL title after defeating debutants Hyderabad Kingsmen by five wickets in the final at Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium on May 3. PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi said the previous edition had set a high benchmark for the league. “HBL PSL 11 showed the world what this league is capable of – thrilling moments that had the whole nation transfixed, record crowds, record broadcasts,” he was quoted as saying in a PCB press release. “HBL PSL 12 will raise the bar further. “We are committed to delivering another outstanding season and look forward to seeing all eight franchises compete once again for the title,” he added. PSL chief executive Salman Naseer said Thursday’s announcement was the beginning of preparations for the next season. “Last season changed what people expect from this league and we intend to meet every one of those expectations in 2027,” he said. “Direct signings, retentions, the trade window and the auction will each bring their own excitement in the months ahead,” he added. The eight franchises — Islamabad United, Karachi Kings, Lahore Qalandars, Multan Sultans, Peshawar Zalmi, Quetta Gladiators, Hyderabad Kingsmen and Rawalpindiz — will now begin preparing for the new season as the PCB works towards finalising the schedule and squad-building process. Further details on the venues, auction and ticketing arrangements will be announced by the PCB in due course

US: Deportations to African Countries Not Their Own
items.description: Click to expand Image “An ICE agent told me to sign for deportation to Chad. I refused . . . The ICE agent said, ‘I don’t care, I’m going to sign it myself.’ . . . I said, ‘I’m going to talk to my lawyer,’ but he said, ‘It’s too late.’ . . . I don’t know what happened, maybe later they changed their minds, because we ended up in Cameroon. . . . Even before we got on the plane, we asked where we were going, and they told us, ‘You’ll find out when you arrive.’” – Tesfay T., 35, an Ethiopian man deported to Cameroon. © 2026 John Holmes for Human Rights Watch The United States has sent more than 500 people whom it cannot deport to their own countries, because of the danger they would face, there to various countries in Africa where they have no connections, without giving them a meaningful chance to contest their removals to these countries.Some of the people have been detained upon arrival. Many, if not most, have been left with no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there.The United States should stop deporting asylum seekers and refugees to third countries that lack the capacity to provide full and fair asylum procedures, and these countries should refuse to receive people under these conditions. (Washington, DC) – The Trump administration is sending hundreds of people who can’t be deported to their own countries, because of the danger they would face, to African countries where they have no connections, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. Many have been left with no practical option but to return to their home countries regardless of the harm they face there. October 8, 2026 “To Scare People” US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa Download the full report in English Appendix I: Third-Country Deportations by the Numbers Appendix II: Response Letters from IOM The 125-page report, “‘To Scare People’: US Expulsions of Third-Country Nationals to Countries in Africa,” documents that US authorities denied the more than 500 people transferred to third countries a meaningful chance to contest their removals or to articulate their fears of being removed to these countries. Some countries arbitrarily detained people they had accepted, and some have sent people onward to the risk of persecution or torture in their home countries, violating the international law principle of nonrefoulement. “Deporting people to countries where they have never set foot is part of a US policy designed to cause human suffering as a means to deter migration,” said Michael Garcia Bochenek, interim US program director at Human Rights Watch. “Because the US government uses these agreements to shirk its responsibilities and to deprive people of their due process rights, the African governments that have entered into these agreements should terminate or suspend them.” Human Rights Watch researchers conducted remote and in some cases in-person interviews between February and July 2026 with 24 third-country nationals transferred from the United States to 6 countries in Africa: Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, and South Sudan. Some of the people sent to these countries face the prospect of persecution and other serious harm in the receiving countries. The United States sent at least a dozen people who identified as lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender (LGBT) to African states that criminalize same-sex relations or public same-sex romantic conduct. These included refugees who had been granted protection in the United States based on the likelihood they would be persecuted in their home countries because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. Their deportation trapped them in situations in which it was neither safe to return home nor possible to obtain effective protection in the third country. Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch The people interviewed consistently described abusive treatment during their flights from the United States, during which they were shackled, sometimes for 18 hours or more, and received little or no information about their destination. How the third-country nationals deported from the United States are treated upon arrival varies from country to country. In some cases, people being deported have not had access to needed medications or treatments for ongoing serious medical conditions. A 35-year-old man from Ethiopia who had fled to the United States after being imprisoned and tortured in his home country had been denied asylum because he had crossed the border irregularly, but a US immigration judge granted him “withholding of removal,” a bar on returning him to Ethiopia because of the likelihood he would again be tortured there. He said that when he refused to sign a voluntary departure form to send him to Chad, an ICE agent signed it himself. “We were chained and handcuffed, legs, hands, stomach” on the flight, he said. “We could not stand up. When I had to use the bathroom, they didn’t even take off the chains.” After arriving in Cameroon, he had repeated visits from representatives of the International Organization for Migration. “Every time they come, they ask the same thing: ‘Do you want to go back to your home?’ But every time I tell them, ‘I’m not going. Stop asking me that. I don’t want to die,’” he told Human Rights Watch in March. The threat of removal to a third country is part of the Trump administration’s policy of mass deportations. In practice, third-country removals have been used to frighten people into leaving before being thrown into the downward spiral of detention and deportation to unknown destinations. An unnamed US official told the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations that in fact, the purpose of third-country national transfers was to terrorize: “With countries like Palau or Eswatini, the point is that the Administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere,” the official said. “The point is to scare people.” The US government violates its domestic and international nonrefoulement obligations by sending people to places where they would face persecution, torture, or certain other serious threats to their lives or safety, or where they would likely be subjected to onward deportations to face such threats, Human Rights Watch said. It also deprives people of a meaningful opportunity to contest their removals to these countries and articulate any risk of abuse they may face if removed there. In December, the US Supreme Court will hear arguments about whether the third-country removal policy violates the Due Process clause of the US constitution or otherwise violates statutory bars against removing people to the risk of being tortured. The court has allowed the government to continue third-country deportations for now. The United States should stop deporting asylum seekers and refugees to third countries that lack the capacity to provide full and fair asylum procedures and in the absence of formal, transparent agreements that ensure they will have access to such procedures. These governments should also respect the principle of nonrefoulement and ensure the dignity, security, and fundamental rights of all persons under their jurisdiction, including third-country nationals whose removal they have accepted. “Several of these African governments are not only complicit in US abuses but have violated the human rights of these deported people themselves, including with arbitrary detention and in some cases sending them back to countries where they fled danger,” Bochenek said. “These countries should not detain people without a clear legal basis, and they should not coerce or send anyone to their home country or another country where they would face a risk of persecution, torture, or other serious harm.”

items.title: Bahrain: Authorities Rearrest Pardoned Detainees
items.description: Click to expand Image Human rights defender, Naji Fateel. © Private (Beirut) – Bahraini authorities have rearrested at least nine men who had previously been released from prison by royal pardon, the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) and Human Rights Watch said today. The men, who were previously detained on politically motivated charges, were arrested in July and August 2026 for allegedly failing to pay fines dating back a decade. Bahraini authorities should immediately release them and cease all efforts to collect the dubious unpaid fines. “King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa’s decision to pardon over 3,000 prisoners in the last two years earned immense praise from the international community, but these new arrests call into question whether the pardons were genuine,” said Niku Jafarnia, Bahrain and Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Those who praised the pardons should call on Bahrain to stop rearresting people and release those again detained.” BIRD and Human Rights Watch spoke to three people, including Naji Fateel, a prominent Bahraini human rights defender who was among the nine rearrested and who spoke from detention. They also spoke to Mustafa al-Jamri and Hassan Burwase, who have not yet been rearrested, but who said the authorities were trying to detain them. The arrests are happening against the backdrop of one of the biggest crackdowns by Bahrain’s authorities on freedom of expression and assembly since the widespread arrests following the 2011 pro-democracy protests. Since March, authorities have arrested over 600 people on various charges, including “supporting and endorsing a state hostile to Bahrain” and espionage, and at least 69 people of Iranian descent have been stripped of their Bahrain nationality, including many children. Those interviewed said the issue was alleged unpaid fines imposed on them and 48 others accused of causing damage during a major protest in Jau Prison in 2015. Human Rights Watch and BIRD have documented that the authorities imposed physical and psychological abuse on the protesters and denied them needed medical care. In 2016, the authorities added 15 years to their sentences and fined them a total of 507,187.97 Bahraini Dinars (approximately US$1.35 million), for offenses including damaging public property, attacking police, arson, and resisting authorities. At the time, BIRD, along with several other human rights organizations, called into question the convictions, saying the Bahraini government had sentenced 57 people to lengthy prison terms amid allegations of abuse, torture, and due process violations, and called on security officials involved in the abuse to be held accountable. The 2024 royal pardons included 33 of those men. All three men interviewed said that their understanding was that the royal pardon also included the charges and fines imposed under the 2016 sentence following the protests. However, in early June, the authorities contacted many of the men to say that they had to pay fines without specifying what the fines were in relation to or how much they should pay. Al-Jamri said that a security official who called him simply said that he had “amounts of money due.” When he asked for clarification, the man said there were “amounts due related to the case,” without any details, and he was told to go to a police station in Manama, the capital. “I was surprised,” al-Jamri said. “What are these amounts? I mean, I hadn’t had any problems; there was nothing against me. I was approaching two years [since my release].” Burwase said the papers linked with his and the rest of the men’s pardons indicated that they had been cleared of “everything, completely,” and that the authorities had also issued him a “good conduct certificate,” meaning there were no outstanding cases against him. On June 16, after hearing from the authorities, 14 of the pardoned men, including the 3 interviewed, wrote to the crown prince, stating their belief that the royal pardon had “brought to an end all consequences arising from the judgments,” including the financial penalties. “This understanding was reinforced by the official measures that followed the pardon and were intended to reintegrate us into society, including government directives to provide training and employment opportunities to those covered by the pardon.” In the letter, the men asked the authorities to recognize the effect of the pardon on the outstanding penalties, halt enforcement measures that could result in their return to prison, clarify their legal position, and ensure that those released under the pardon were not imprisoned simply because they could not afford to pay any outstanding fines. The men received no response. But in July and August, the authorities arrested 8 of the 33 convicted in 2016 and pardoned in 2024. Among them, three were signatories to the letter. Fateel said that on August 16, officials contacted him regarding the fine. He had asked them to provide documentation establishing the amount to be paid and whether he should go to the police station to discuss the matter. He said that the officials had told him to instead contact the public prosecution and the sentence enforcement judge, who oversees sentencing for convicted individuals. He said that plainclothes officers awakened him at approximately 5:45 a.m. on August 18, banging loudly on his bedroom door. He said they immediately arrested him and took him away without explaining the reason for his arrest or presenting a warrant. He said that when they were headed to the East Riffa Police Station, an officer told him that he had been arrested because of “a fine.” In 2022, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found Fateel’s original detention arbitrary and therefore unlawful, concluding that the proceedings involved serious violations of international fair-trial standards. They called for his immediate and unconditional release. The findings covered the Jau Prison case now being used by authorities to rearrest him. By the time he was finally released in 2024, Fateel had spent 11 years in arbitrary detention. Fateel, along with many others who had been pardoned, now faces imprisonment again for fines that he should not in fact be liable for and cannot afford, the groups said. Regarding the exorbitant amount of the fine, al-Jamri said: “It would be difficult for anyone in Bahrain to pay, whether they had a case against them or not. A salary in Bahrain might be 350 dinars [a month], yet you’re asking me to pay installments of 375 dinars [every month] for two years.” As of October 5, Bahraini authorities have continued to pursue arrests for others from the 33 people convicted in 2016 and released in 2024, based on reports from some of those who authorities have contacted. “Bahrain’s government is going after former political prisoners released by royal pardon, giving them a difficult choice: pay huge fines or go back to prison,” said Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, advocacy director at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy. “The EU, UK, and US rushed to applaud Bahrain for releasing political prisoners. They should now speak out and call on Bahrain to cease targeting those who were released.”

items.title: Blogger Jailed for Four Years in Uzbekistan
items.description: Blogger Sirojiddin Adilov’s October 5 conviction on dubious extortion and fraud charges raises serious questions about fair trial standards in Uzbekistan, as well as the government’s commitment to upholding freedom of expression. Click to expand Image Sirojiddin Adilov, September 2026. © 2026 Abdurakhmon Tashanov A criminal court sentenced Adilov—who ran “Sirojiddin Media,” a YouTube channel with over 915,000 subscribers—to four years in a prison colony for committing extortion in the case of one individual and fraud in the case of two others. The court also ordered that he pay a total of 75 million Som in damages (approximately US $6370). The court explicitly noted that Adilov was not prosecuted in connection with his social media activities. Yet, Adilov’s arrest in March 2026 came just several months after he reported on a case of abuse of power in law enforcement, raising concerns that he may have been targeted for his critical reporting. The human rights organization Ezgulik reported on multiple procedural violations in Adilov’s case, including authorities’ refusal to allow Adilov to choose his own lawyer in pretrial detention proceedings and a warrantless police search of Adilov’s apartment and vehicle. The head of Ezgulik, Abdurakhman Tashanov, who monitored Adilov’s trial, informed Human Rights Watch that none of the individuals who filed complaints against Adilov provided substantiating evidence to support their claims. Tashanov also pointed out that from the time of the alleged incidents of fraud and extortion, it took the complainants over three years to file a complaint. Adilov’s “Sirojiddin Media” reported in 2025 on the efforts of a school principal from the Fergana region, Gulirano Kosimova, to hold accountable police officers who had beat her and made her strip naked on camera as part of an apparent set up to frame another official. In late November 2025, Kosimova won her case and a Fergana district criminal court convicted a district police chief and his deputy, sentencing them to four years in a prison colony. Adilov’s sentencing comes amidst increasing restrictions on freedom of expression in Uzbekistan. Authorities should stop prosecuting bloggers and others on dubious extortion charges and for non-violent offenses such as “insulting the president online.” Sirojiddin Adilov was entitled to a fair trial and should get a fair and impartial appeals hearing that respects due process and is capable of reviewing both the procedural aspects and evidence base of his conviction.

items.title: Peshawar High Court rejects Afridi’s plea challenging ECP proceedings
items.description: • Judge advises KP CM’s counsel to let the commission hear him first • Chief minister accused of violating code of conduct in Haripur by-polls last year • Petitioner’s lawyers say the process initiated by ECP may result in his disqualification PESHAWAR: The Peshawar High Court on Wednesday rejected a petition filed by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi challenging proceedings initiated against him by the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) for allegedly violating the election code of conduct during by-elections in Haripur in November 2025. A bench comprising Justice Syed Arshad Ali and Justice Muhammad Faheem Wali pronounced a short order dismissing the petition without touching the question of the ECP’s jurisdiction in light of an earlier court order. The detailed judgement will be issued later. With the dismissal of the petition, a stay order earlier granted in favour of Mr Afridi also stands vacated. Following the preliminary hearing of the petition earlier this year, the court had ordered, “In the meanwhile, the respondent-ECP may proceed with the matter; however, it shall not pass any final order adverse to the petitioner (Sohail Afridi) till further orders.” The development assumes significance amid growing tensions between KP and federal governments over the ongoing protest march. A panel of lawyers appeared for the petitioner, including Adnan Ali, Bashir Khan Wazir, Barrister Sarwar Muzaffar Shah and Inam Yousafzai. The ECP was represented by Additional Director General (Law) Khurram Shehzad and Additional Director (Law) Samran Jehangir, while Barrister Sajeel Sheharyar Swati appeared for the complainant against Mr Afridi before the ECP. In November last year, the chief minister and by-election candidate Shehrnaz Omar Ayub, backed by PTI, had challenged notices issued to them by the ECP for allegedly violating the election code of conduct. Mr Afridi had challenged a notice issued to him by the ECP on Nov 20, accusing him of delivering a provocative speech against government functionaries in connection with the by-election in NA-18 Haripur. The ECP contended that the CM’s speech was contrary to the code of conduct issued by the commission for the by-election. Mr Afridi had asked the high court to set aside the impugned notice. However, on Nov 26, the court dismissed both petitions, observing that no adverse order had so far been passed against the petitioners. The bench had observed that it expected the ECP, in the first instance, to determine its jurisdiction in the matter before proceeding further with the inquiry. Mr Afridi again approached the court earlier this year, contending that the ECP had been proceeding against him without first deciding the question of its jurisdiction, contrary to the Elections Act, 2017. ECP counsel Khurram Shehzad argued that the petition was not maintainable and was liable to be dismissed as no order had so far been passed against the petitioner. He submitted that the proceedings pending before the commission were independent in nature and separate from those pending before the district monitoring officer (DMO). He argued that the ECP had two types of jurisdiction — one concerning civil wrongs and the other concerning cases of a criminal nature. Under Section 15 of the Elections Act, 2017, he said, the ECP could take cognisance of matters relating to implementation of the code of conduct on its own motion as well as on a complaint filed by an aggrieved person. He contended that an almost identical petition had been dismissed by the court in November last year. Mr Afridi’s counsel, Adnan Ali, stated that the ECP had issued the controversial notice to the chief minister on Nov 20, 2025. “The allegation pertained to remarks made against election staff and influencing the election,” he said. “The speech delivered by the chief minister was outside the jurisdiction of NA-18 Haripur, where the by-election was held on Nov 23, 2025,” the counsel argued. He said that once the DMO had issued a notice to Mr Afridi under Section 234 of the Elections Act, the ECP lacked jurisdiction to issue another notice to him under Section 15 of the Act. He argued that the ECP had clubbed a private complaint filed by a rival candidate with its suo motu proceedings. He contended that the ECP was exercising the powers of the DMO. “Here, both the ECP and the DMO issued notices, and the DMO also submitted a report to the former,” he argued. “Let the Election Commission hear you; present whatever your response is before them,” Justice Arshad Ali remarked. The bench observed, “This is merely an inquiry by the Election Commission, not a formal action. There is no legal bar preventing the Election Commission from conducting an inquiry.” However, Mr Afridi’s lawyers maintained that the ECP had initiated a process under which the petitioner could face disqualification. Published in Dawn, October 8th, 2026

items.title: Pepe Álvarez: “No es una huelga clásica”; Unai Sordo: “La chispa es Maricarmen”
items.description: La gran oleada de protestas desatada en España por la crisis de la vivienda ha cristalizado en pocos días en dos movimientos inesperados: elecciones anticipadas y huelga general, ambas en noviembre. Conscientes de la excepcionalidad del momento —y de la fuerza del movimiento en las calles—, Unai Sordo (Barakaldo, Bizkaia, 54 años) y Pepe Álvarez (Belmonte de Miranda, Asturias, 70 años) han decidido afrontar el 11 de noviembre su primera huelga general al frente de sus respectivos sindicatos, CC OO y UGT, las dos grandes centrales del país. Estas organizaciones, junto al Sindicato de Inquilinas, otros sindicatos a la izquierda de los tradicionales y algunos de carácter autonómico , llaman a los trabajadores a movilizarse por los problemas de acceso a la vivienda, una reivindicación alejada de los parámetros clásicos de los paros laborales. Este miércoles, Sordo y Álvarez verbalizaron a EL PAÍS, por separado en sus respectivos despachos, las razones que han motivado esta decisión. Las entrevistas se produjeron horas antes de conocerse la muerte de Maricarmen, la mujer de 87 años cuyo desahucio en Madrid ha desencadenado toda la movilización social. La importancia de su caso vertebró buena parte de la conversación con los dos dirigentes. Seguir leyendo

Son cuatro extractos de una serie de mensajes publicados por Rafael Palacios, alias Rafapal , el 30 de abril de 2019, dos días después de las primeras generales en las que Pedro Sánchez consiguió ser el candidato más votado . La misma línea siguió una alerta difundida por Luis Pérez, alias Alvise , algo menos de dos años después, durante la precampaña de unas autonómicas madrileñas: “Si podéis NO VOTÉIS POR CORREO”. items.description: Pedro Sánchez fue muy claro este martes, tras un Consejo de Ministros que aprobó dos decretos de emergencia sobre vivienda: “El Gobierno va a continuar gobernando”. El Ejecutivo no está en funciones hasta que se vote, tiene plenitud de facultades, y además tiene la ventaja de que lo que apruebe se convalida en la Diputación Permanente , un órgano donde Junts no es imprescindible, basta con lograr el apoyo del PNV además del de los socios de izquierdas de la coalición PSOE-Sumar (ERC, Bildu y Podemos). Por eso, el Ejecutivo está estudiando diversas posibilidades para explotar hasta el último momento la gran ventaja de controlar el Boletín Oficial del Estado, esto es, poder aprobar medidas sociales hasta el último día. Los ministerios y La Moncloa trabajan en distintas ideas, que irán desplegándose a lo largo de las semanas, según fuentes del Ejecutivo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Alquila a un humano: el futuro en el que las IA contratan personas para hacer trabajos físicos ya está aquí
items.description: El artista húngaro Peter Weiler quería probar una nueva plataforma llamada RentAHuman, literalmente “alquila a un humano”. El lema de la web es “mano de obra física para la IA” y es para que agentes de inteligencia artificial contraten a personas para hacer trabajos. Weiler quiso probar la plataforma y ofreció dinero para que un humano sostuviera un cartel en una plaza del centro de Budapest con este texto en húngaro e inglés: “Una IA me contrató para este trabajo”. items.title: ¿Quién ganará el Nobel de Literatura? Cómo han cambiado los premiados y quién es favorito en 2026
items.description: Hay muy pocas certezas sobre quién ganará el Premio Nobel de Literatura de 2026, que se falla este jueves por la mañana, pero en el primer puesto de todas las listas de predicciones –a pocas horas para la ceremonia de entrega– aparece la escritora Can Xue (China, 73 años). Con sus relatos cortos de ficción “experimental”, según describe la crítica, la autora tiene de media cerca de un 16% de probabilidades de ganar el galardón. Teniendo en cuenta que es la favorita, es un porcentaje muy bajo: ni siquiera alcanza una de cada cinco opciones de obtener el premio. No obstante, se sitúa a seis puntos por delante del siguiente favorito, Gerald Murnane. Les siguen muy de cerca Anne Carson, Amitav Ghosh y otros cinco aspirantes con probabilidades similares. items.title: El Gobierno registra 11.000 retornos de migrantes de Ceuta a Marruecos en dos meses
items.description: Los desalojos efectuados por la Policía Nacional en las playas de Benítez y de El Trampolín, en Ceuta, han desembocado en cientos y cientos de “retornos voluntarios” a Marruecos, acelerando el ritmo de salidas exponencialmente. Más de 2.500 migrantes han abandonado la ciudad autónoma en una semana, durante y después de los operativos policiales para desmantelar los asentamientos, según cifras actualizadas por La Moncloa, a las que ha accedido EL PAÍS. Está previsto que este jueves el ministro Ángel Víctor Torres, al frente del mando único desde el 25 de agosto, desgrane los datos en una comparecencia de prensa en la Delegación de Gobierno tras la reunión semanal del Comité de Situación. En total, desde el 10 de agosto han regresado a Marruecos unas 11.000 personas que llegaron en el cruce masivo (entre las que se incluye también las devoluciones por infracción, que no superan las 500). Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los 100 bulos de Ceuta: migrantes que llegan por túneles, agua en mal estado y falsas entradas masivas
items.description: “Decían que habían entrado 800 migrantes por Benzú, pero al hacer una inspección por el monte solo se veían unas cabras”, cuenta un agente de Ceuta. El 23 de septiembre, día en el que se celebraban las elecciones parlamentarias en Marruecos, la ciudad volvía a estar en vilo ante el temor de que repitiera una entrada masiva como la de los 30 y 31 de julio, en la que unas 80.000 personas accedieron a la ciudad en cuestión de horas. Un falso aviso de entrada, de entre 200 y 800 personas, según los mensajes, corrió por los chats y canales de Whatsapp de vecinos y puso en alerta a los medios. Varias fuentes policiales negaron que hubiera llegado a cruzar alguna persona, pero la noticia salió en varias televisiones. Hubo un intento de entrada de algo más de un centenar de migrantes, que se frenó desde Marruecos, pero esta información ni corrió, ni caló tan rápido como la inicial. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El caos se enquista en Rodalies con un nuevo pulso de los maquinistas
items.description: La red de Rodalies de Cataluña no es solo un servicio que acumula una endémica falta de inversiones que generan problemas de todo tipo a sus usuarios cada día. Este miércoles volvió a poner en evidencia que es también un tablero sobre el que se juega un fiero pulso entre la Generalitat (esta vez con las empresas estatales Adif y Renfe a su lado) y los maquinistas, a quienes representa el sindicato mayoritario Semaf. La oposición de los conductores de trenes a circular con el argumento de la falta de seguridad acabó torciendo el brazo de las administraciones, que vieron cómo por quinto día consecutivo, y sin necesidad de ningún mensaje ES-Alert como aviso preventivo, el servicio ferroviario de corta distancia quedaba paralizado a primera hora de la mañana y los conductores de los trenes lograban lo que reclamaban: informes adicionales que garantizaran la seguridad de la infraestructura. En resumen, la enésima jornada consecutiva de caos en el servicio ferroviario de Cataluña. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Carlos Briones, divulgador: “No podemos dejar un móvil a un chaval para que no moleste y luego reprocharle que le dedique horas”
items.description: No es la primera vez, ni mucho menos, que Carlos Briones (Burgos, 57 años) recibe un premio : en 1993, cuando aún nada hacía intuir que acabaría siendo uno de los divulgadores científicos más prestigiosos de España, ganó el Hiperión por su talento como poeta. “Llegué a recitar con Ángel González dos veces. Tengo mil anécdotas. Es parte de mi riqueza”. En aquella época también tocaba un violín que su padre había llevado un día a casa. Solo dejó el conservatorio cuando después de terminar ciencias químicas, la tesis que desarrolló en el Centro de Biología Molecular Severo Ochoa le quitó todo el tiempo. “¡No era precisamente Ara Malikian !”. Después, ya como coordinador de un grupo que investiga sobre el origen y la evolución temprana de la vida en el Centro de Astrobiología (CSNI-INTA)—su trabajo principal actual—, fue reconocido por la NASA por su contribución a la caracterización de la biosfera subterránea de nuestro planeta. Ahora, el Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Científicas (CSIC) y la Fundación BBVA han premiado su indudable capacidad para contagiar al gran público la curiosidad por absolutamente todo lo que ayuda a responder las grandes preguntas. Seguir leyendo

items.title: ¿Puede la ficción reconciliarte con tu padre? “Pensaba que no le quería hasta que escribí sobre él”
items.description: “La única indicación que les había dado era que se despidieran, y entonces pasó eso”, recuerda Carlos Saiz, director de Lionel , sobre una de las escenas finales de su película, en la que los protagonistas son capaces de hablar de cuestiones que hasta el momento solo habían provocado incomodidad o violencia. “Fue como una catarsis terapéutica y me puse a llorar tanto que tuve que dar la vuelta a la manzana porque me daba vergüenza que el resto del equipo me viera así, pero casi todos lloramos en ese momento”, continúa. Lionel , estrenada el 11 de septiembre, narra la historia de Lionel Corral (algo más de 50 años) y Lionel Corral (unos 25), un padre y un hijo distanciados desde hace años que se interpretan a sí mismos mientras completan un viaje (de Murcia a Francia y de vuelta a Murcia en un Peugeot destartalado) que realmente hicieron durante el rodaje. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Los que decidieron atacar a una anciana desahuciada: “Era una jeta”, “jugaba al bingo”, “si fuera Morocarmen tendría casa”
items.description: El caso de Maricarmen ha movilizado y removido la conciencia de todo un país , pero también ha sacado lo peor de él. La mujer expulsada de su vivienda recibió odio y desdén desde el momento en que fue desahuciada de su casa hace dos semanas —lo que la convirtió en un símbolo de la crisis de la vivienda en España— hasta hace unas pocas horas, cuando se anunció que había muerto en el hospital a los 87 años de edad. La han tratado de retratar como una caradura que se aprovechaba de su edad, que fingía estar enferma. Han ido a entrevistar a sus vecinos para demostrar que no saludaba por la calle, que se gastaba el dinero en el bingo o que se quejaba demasiado cuando no funcionaba el ascensor. Bajo el disfraz de anciana indefensa, decían, se escondía un lobo. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La cuenta atrás fue más rápida para Maricarmen
items.description: Faltaban 24 horas para el desahucio de Mariano y la entrevista en el salón de su casa de Vallecas había comenzado bien. Descafeinado de un sorbo, empezó a hablar de forma tranquila y coherente sobre la casa en la que vivía desde los tres años, la infancia junto a sus padres, dejar su casa a los 58 años... hasta que se le empezó a cortar la voz y se detuvo. items.title: KP CM Afridi seeks law to impeach governor, rejects operations
items.description: • KP CM tells chief secretary, police chief not to follow ‘unconstitutional’ orders • Insists Centre’s counterterrorism approach failed; claims KP can restore peace within 100 days • Joins march supporters in Bara; says future strategy to be announced in Swabi • Kundi says governor’s rule, emergency will be imposed ‘to save KP’ PESHAWAR: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Wednesday took strong exception to Governor Faisal Karim Kundi’s meeting with the chief secretary and provincial police chief and called for legislation to provide for the governor’s impeachment for “violating the Constitution”. “A prime minister and the chief minister can be sent home through a vote of no confidence. If there is no law, the KP Assembly will legislate [for impeachment of the governor] and nobody will be allowed to derail democracy,” Mr Afridi said. In a video message shared by his office, the chief minister accused the governor of acting unconstitutionally and attempting to provoke the provincial government but said his administration would continue to abide by the law and Constitution. “We will follow the Con­s­titution and that hurts ‘them’,” Mr Afridi said while chairing a meeting of the provincial cabinet. His remarks came a day after Governor Kundi cha­i­red a meeting with Chief Secretary Shahab Ali Shah and KP Police Chief Zulfiqar Hameed on the province’s security situation. Mr Afridi urged the two officials not to comply with any unconstitutional or illegal order from anyone. KP Advocate General Shah Faisal Utmankhel told the meeting that under Article 131 of the Constitution, the governor could seek information from the chief minister, but could not do so independently. “If I do not order you to take an unconstitutional step, do not obey if someone pushes you to follow any unconstitutional order,” Mr Afridi said. The chief minister direc­ted the chief secretary to advise the provincial admi­n­i­stration against involvement in any unconstitutional activity and ordered the inspector general of police to investigate firing on PTI workers in Upper South Waziristan. Mr Afridi accused the PPP-affiliated governor of staging a “drama” by convening the security meeting and termed the move unconstitutional. He said the provincial assembly, cabinet and government were fully functional and that such a meeting was unacceptable when the provincial government enjoyed a two-thirds majority. Turning his criticism towards the PPP, Mr Afridi blamed former president Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, along with Gen Yahya Khan, for the separation of East Pakistan and accused President Asif Ali Zardari of seeking to create a similar situation. “We will not allow any conspiracy to break up Pakistan to succeed,” he said, alleging that the PPP had always prioritised personal interests over national interests. Kundi raises governor’s rule Meanwhile, Governor Kundi said later on Wednesday that an emergency or governor’s rule would “definitely” be imposed in KP if the prime minister and the president considered it necessary to “save the province” amid the security situation. Speaking to Geo News , Mr Kundi said there had been precedents for the imposition of an emergency or governor’s rule. “In Balochistan, the PPP had to end its government for law and order and impose an emergency,” he said. Asked whether such a measure would be sustainable if imposed in KP, Mr Kundi said, “The first thing [to decide] is when and whether it is imposed. We can discuss its sustainability in another programme.” Counterterrorism policy Mr Afridi also reiterated his opposition to the Centre’s counterterrorism policy and said his government would not allow further military operations in the province. He maintained that terrorism had again been “imposed on the province” and said his government had worked to strengthen the police, Counter-Terrorism Depar­tment and Special Branch since he took office on Oct 15, 2025. Mr Afridi alleged that successive federal governments had imposed military operations on KP since 2004, displacing people who had still not received full compensation. He claimed nearly Rs100bn in compensation remained outstanding and said tribal families displaced from their homes had been promised Rs400,000 per household, but many had yet to receive the full amount. He also referred to a commitment to provide Rs370m to Rs380m a month to displaced people from North Waziristan living at the Baka Khel camp, stressing that the promised payments were still not being made. Mr Afridi said KP was fighting terrorism while also dealing with the consequences of federal policies and claimed peace could be restored within 100 days if the approach advocated by provincial stakeholders was adopted. He argued that the Centre’s counterterrorism policy had failed to bring peace either in KP or Balochistan and called for a change in approach. “A shift in policy is necessary. KP can establish peace within 100 days,” he said. Later on Wednesday, PTI workers from Bara, Jamrud and Landi Kotal welcomed the chief minister in his hometown of Bara as he travelled towards Peshawar as part of the party’s march. Addressing supporters from the top of a truck, Mr Afridi said no pressure tactic could weaken his resolve and again vowed not to allow further military operations in KP. He said the rights of the province would be pursued and announced that the future strategy for the march would be unveiled on reaching Swabi. The chief minister and participants in the march were expected to stay overnight in Bara before leaving for Peshawar on Thursday (today). Cabinet decisions The provincial cabinet approved forwarding to the federal government a joint resolution adopted by the KP Assembly condemning an incident in which the chief minister was allegedly taken away by Punjab Police in a vehicle, separated from his security detail and later left on the roadside without security during a visit to Punjab. The cabinet also approved obtaining $250m in World Bank financing for the READY-KP project under the bank’s applicable financing terms. Our correspondent in Khyber also contributed to this report Published in Dawn, October 8th, 2026

Cette mission s’inscrit dans une feuille de route de six mois, adoptée en juillet pour accompagner le processus de paix dans l’est de la RDC. items.title: Portugal registers hottest September on record
items.description: Portugal experienced its hottest September this year since records started in 1931, the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA) said on Wednesday. It said the average air temperature was 23.4 degrees Celsius, some 2.9 degrees Celsius higher than the average for 1991-2020, "making this month of September the hottest since 1931," the IPMA said in a statement. "The maximum air temperature reached 31.03 degrees Celsius, about 4.21 degrees Celsius above the norm, which is again the highest of a historic series," it added. Portugal was hit by two hot spells during the month, according to the agency, which said September was the fifth driest for rainfall since 2000. The country recorded its highest temperature for the month of May this year, reaching 40.3 degrees Celsius. The IPMA said last week that it had been the third warmest summer on record.

items.title: France holds talks with Taliban govt on deporting Afghans
items.description: PARIS: France has begun talks with the Taliban government to “facilitate” the deportation of Afghan citizens to Afghanistan, a diplomatic source said on Wednesday. Paris has had no diplomatic relations with the Taliban authorities since their return to power in August 2021, and its embassy in Kabul remains closed. But it has joined about 20 EU countries including Germany, Belgium and Sweden to speed up the return of Afghans, specifically those who have been convicted by courts. “As in other European countries, a technical dialogue has been initiated with the Taliban in order to facilitate the direct removal to Afghanistan of Afghan nationals in an irregular situation who pose a threat to public order,” the source said. The Taliban authorities, which are not officially recognised by the European Union, are seeking to strengthen their international standing. France’s foreign ministry did not respond to questions on whether Taliban representatives would be able to visit the country to accelerate procedures. The diplomatic source did not specify the number of individuals who could be deported, but another source familiar with the matter said it could be “hundreds”. “This technical dialogue does not call our position on Afghanistan into question,” the diplomatic source said, adding: “And we are maintaining our support for the Afghan population, and in particular for Afghan women.” A June meeting between Taliban government officials and EU lawmakers sparked criticism from human rights organisations and left-leaning groups in the European parliament. Since returning to power, the Taliban has imposed a strict version of Islamic law on Afghanistan. Women are particularly affected, being banned from public places and most jobs, while education for girls beyond age 12 is outlawed. Published in Dawn, October 8th, 2026
